metadata.narrative: Write a blog post contrasting Euclidean geometry used in high school math competitions such as the AMC, AIME, or Olympiads to geometry taught in the standard American high school math curriculums. This post is written for people with knowledge of geometry from standard high school classes, but with no math experience in competitive math. Your post must include clear examples of problem solving techniques and theorems that are commonly used in high school math competitions, but not typically taught in a high school math class.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: If you learned geometry in a typical American public high school, you spent a year proving triangle congruence, working with similarity and right-triangle trigonometry, exploring circle theorems, translating between coordinate equations and conic sections, computing volumes with formulas like Cavalieri's principle, and modeling real objects with geometric shapes.
That is essentially the Common Core geometry sequence, taught largely through transformations and a handful of named theorems about parallel lines, triangles, and parallelograms.
Students in that class rarely see anything beyond the inscribed angle theorem, the Pythagorean theorem, and the law of cosines applied to circles and triangles.

Competition geometry on the AMC, AIME, and Olympiads such as USAMO or the IMO uses the same objects, triangles and circles, but draws on a much larger and more specialized toolbox that a regular class never opens.

One veteran Olympiad coach's advice to students preparing for international competitions is to "learn enough Euclidean Geometry to be on good terms with Simson's Theorem, Ceva's theorem, excircles, Menelaus's theorem, power of a point and the radical axis theorem," none of which appear in a standard curriculum.

Commercial competition-prep courses make the contrast explicit, separating a "Pre-AP Geometry curriculum" track from a "Geometry for Competitions" track that adds Ceva's, Menelaus', and Stewart's theorems, power of a point, inversion, vectors, and geometric transformations aimed at AMC and AIME-level problems.

Advanced Olympiad-prep syllabi build outward from "Fundamentals: Similar Triangles, Power of a Point, and Cyclic Quadrilaterals" into homothety, locus, concurrence, collinearity, three-dimensional geometry, and inversion, an entire second curriculum layered on top of the first.

This gap is not hypothetical: one geometry reference notes that "in recent years, the AIME has included advanced geometry problems of an olympiad flavor," meaning the exam has drifted further from classroom material over time.

The clearest example of a competition-only tool is the power of a point, which says that for a point P and a circle, any line through P intersecting the circle at two points A and B gives a product PA·PB depending only on P and the circle, with a negative sign convention when P is inside the circle.

This fact turns messy configurations with intersecting chords, secants, and tangent lines into one-line algebra, and it also underlies the radical axis theorem: for two non-concentric circles, points of equal power with respect to both form a straight line, and the three radical axes of three circles are always concurrent at a radical center.

A representative Mock AIME problem uses this idea directly, showing that a point equidistant in power from two circles lies on their radical axis, forcing collinearity and an altitude relationship that collapses a long synthetic argument into a short computation.

A second staple is Ptolemy's theorem, which states that for any cyclic quadrilateral ABCD the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides, AC·BD = AB·CD + BC·AD, along with its converse characterizing cyclic quadrilaterals.

A clean illustration is the corollary for an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle: for any point P on that circle, the distance to the farthest vertex equals the sum of the distances to the two nearer vertices, a fact that falls out of Ptolemy's relation in one line.

A third tool, Ceva's theorem, tells you exactly when three cevians from a triangle's vertices are concurrent, via the product condition on the ratios they cut on the opposite sides, and it is commonly proved using ratios of triangle areas sharing a common vertex, training students to see ratios geometrically rather than only algebraically.

Stewart's theorem generalizes this cevian idea by giving the exact length of any cevian: for a cevian from A to point D on BC with BD = y and DC = x, the relation b²y + c²x = a(d² + xy) holds, specializing cleanly to formulas for medians, angle bisectors, and altitudes.

Competitors often skip these length formulas in favor of mass point geometry, a technique borrowed from physics that assigns weights to a triangle's vertices so cevians balance like a see-saw, letting a solver read length ratios directly off the masses instead of building similar triangles or coordinate equations.
A worked example assigns a mass of 3 to one vertex and 1 to each of the other two, instantly yielding the intersection ratios along two cevians without any trigonometry.

For circle-heavy Olympiad problems, spiral similarity, a mapping built from a rotation and a scaling sharing one fixed center, gives a way to map one segment onto another and is explicitly the tool of choice in published solutions to International Mathematical Olympiad and other national olympiad problems, often alongside inversion and the Apollonius circle.

Real AIME problems make the practical difference obvious: contestants are asked to find a length inside a triangle with a circle intersecting all three sides under a given ratio condition, or to relate tangent circles nested inside a larger circle with prescribed radius ratios.
These problems assume fluency with power of a point, tangent-circle relationships, and algebraic manipulation of radicals well beyond a typical circle-theorems unit.

Put together, these examples show that competition geometry is not simply a harder version of the same class, but a parallel curriculum built around synthetic shortcuts, area and ratio arguments, and named classical theorems that let a solver bypass heavy coordinate bookkeeping under time pressure.

A standard high school class rewards careful, step-by-step proof and formula application within the six Common Core units of congruence, similarity, circles, coordinate geometry, measurement, and modeling.

AMC, AIME, and Olympiad geometry instead rewards pattern recognition, the instinct to reach for Ptolemy, Ceva, Stewart, power of a point, mass points, radical axes, or spiral similarity the moment a configuration calls for it, and comfort moving fluidly between synthetic and trigonometric arguments in a way ordinary coursework simply does not train.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

If you learned geometry in a typical American public high school, you spent a year proving triangle congruence, working with similarity and right-triangle trigonometry, exploring circle theorems, translating between coordinate equations and conic sections, computing volumes with formulas like Cavalieri's principle, and modeling real objects with geometric shapes.
That is essentially the Common Core geometry sequence: congruence, similarity/right triangles/trigonometry, circles, coordinate geometry, measurement and dimension, and modeling, taught largely through transformations and a handful of named theorems about parallel lines, triangles, and parallelograms.
Students in that class rarely see anything beyond the inscribed angle theorem, the Pythagorean theorem, and the law of cosines applied to circles and triangles.
Competition geometry on the AMC, AIME, and Olympiads such as USAMO or the IMO uses the exact same objects, points, lines, triangles, and circles, but draws on a much larger and more specialized toolbox that a regular class never opens.
One veteran Olympiad coach's blunt advice to students preparing for international competitions is to "learn enough Euclidean Geometry to be on good terms with Simson's Theorem, Ceva's theorem, excircles, Menelaus's theorem, power of a point and the radical axis theorem," none of which appear in a standard curriculum.
Commercial competition-prep courses make the contrast explicit, separating a "Pre-AP Geometry curriculum" track from a "Geometry for Competitions" track that adds Ceva's, Menelaus', and Stewart's theorems, power of a point, inversion, vectors, and geometric transformations aimed specifically at AMC and AIME-level problems.
Even the most advanced Olympiad-prep syllabi build outward from "Fundamentals: Similar Triangles, Power of a Point, and Cyclic Quadrilaterals" into homothety, locus, concurrence, collinearity, three-dimensional geometry, and inversion, an entire second curriculum layered on top of the first.
This gap is not hypothetical: one geometry reference source notes plainly that "in recent years, the AIME has included advanced geometry problems of an olympiad flavor," meaning the exam has drifted further from classroom material over time.
The clearest example of a competition-only tool is the power of a point, which says that for a point P and a circle, any line through P intersecting the circle at two points A and B gives a product PA·PB that depends only on P and the circle, not on the particular line chosen, with a negative sign convention when P is inside the circle.
This single fact turns messy configurations with intersecting chords, secants, and tangent lines into one-line algebra, and it also underlies the radical axis theorem, which states that for two non-concentric circles, the locus of points having equal power with respect to both circles is a straight line, and that the three radical axes of three circles are always concurrent at a single radical center.
A representative Mock AIME problem uses exactly this idea: two circles and a point Q equidistant from their radical axis let a solver show that certain segments are collinear and an altitude of a triangle is perpendicular to the line joining the centers, collapsing what looks like a three-page synthetic proof into a short power-of-a-point argument.
A second staple is Ptolemy's theorem, which states that for any cyclic quadrilateral ABCD the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides, AC·BD = AB·CD + BC·AD, together with its converse that this equality characterizes cyclic quadrilaterals.
A clean illustration is the corollary for an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle: if P is any point on that circle, the distance from P to the farthest vertex equals the sum of the distances to the two nearer vertices, a fact that falls out of Ptolemy's relation in one line but has no natural home in a standard-curriculum unit on circles.
A third tool, Ceva's theorem, tells you exactly when three cevians drawn from the vertices of a triangle to the opposite sides are concurrent, via the product condition (AD/DB)(BE/EC)(CF/FA) = 1, and it is commonly proved using ratios of triangle areas that share a common vertex, a technique that trains students to see ratios geometrically rather than only algebraically.
Stewart's theorem generalizes this cevian idea by giving the exact length of any cevian, stating that for a cevian from A to point D on BC with BD = y and DC = x, the relation b²y + c²x = a(d² + xy) holds, which then specializes cleanly to formulas for medians, angle bisectors, and altitudes depending on what kind of cevian is drawn.
Competitors often skip these length formulas entirely in favor of mass point geometry, a technique borrowed from physics that assigns weights to a triangle's vertices so that cevians balance like a see-saw, letting a solver read length ratios directly off the masses instead of setting up similar triangles or coordinate equations, as shown in worked examples where assigning a mass of 3 to one vertex and 1 to each of the other two instantly yields the ratios along two intersecting cevians.
For circle-heavy Olympiad problems, spiral similarity, a mapping built from a rotation and a scaling sharing one fixed center, gives a way to map one segment onto another and is explicitly the tool of choice in solutions to International Mathematical Olympiad and other national olympiad problems, often alongside inversion and the Apollonius circle, concepts that also never surface in a standard class.
Real AIME problems make the practical difference obvious: contestants are asked to find a length inside a triangle with a circle intersecting all three sides under a given ratio condition, or to relate tangent circles nested inside a larger circle with prescribed radius ratios, problems that assume fluency with power of a point, tangent-circle relationships, and algebraic manipulation of radicals well beyond a typical circle-theorems unit.
Put together, these examples show that competition geometry is not a harder version of the same class so much as a parallel curriculum built around synthetic shortcuts, area and ratio arguments, and named classical theorems that let a solver bypass heavy coordinate bookkeeping under real time pressure.
A standard high school class rewards careful, step-by-step proof and formula application, while AMC, AIME, and Olympiad geometry rewards pattern recognition, the ability to reach for Ptolemy, Ceva, Stewart, power of a point, mass points, radical axes, or spiral similarity the moment a configuration calls for it, and comfort moving fluidly between synthetic and trigonometric arguments in a way ordinary coursework simply does not train.
